fields.title: How NSE & BSE Work
fields.summary: India's two main stock exchanges and how trades actually happen.
fields.body_html:
What is a stock exchange, really?

A stock exchange is a regulated marketplace where people buy and sell shares of publicly listed companies. India has two major ones: the NSE (National Stock Exchange, founded 1994) and the BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange, founded 1875 — Asia's oldest). Both operate fully electronically today.

Both exchanges are regulated by SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India), which was established in 1992 and has the legal authority to make rules, investigate fraud, and penalise wrongdoers.

The lifecycle of a trade

  1. You place an order on your broker's app (Zerodha, Groww, Upstox, Dhan, etc.). This broker is a SEBI-registered intermediary.
  2. The broker routes it to the exchange's matching engine. If you placed a market order, it executes at the best available counter-price. A limit order sits in the order book until matched.
  3. Clearing happens via NSE Clearing / ICCL — the counterparty to every trade, removing the risk that the other side defaults.
  4. Settlement is T+1 — shares land in your demat account one working day after the trade, and cash is debited from the buyer.

NSE vs BSE — which should you care about?

For most retail investors, it barely matters. The same stock usually trades on both, often at near-identical prices (arbitrage keeps them in sync). Differences:

  • NSE handles ~90%+ of equity cash-market volume. Its flagship index is the Nifty 50.
  • BSE is older and home to the Sensex (30 stocks). It lists more small and mid-caps.
  • Derivatives (F&O) are dominated by NSE.

Trading hours you need to know

  • Pre-open session: 9:00 – 9:15 AM (price discovery)
  • Normal market: 9:15 AM – 3:30 PM
  • Closing session: 3:30 – 4:00 PM (closing prices determined)
  • Markets are closed on weekends and published holidays.

A note on “circuits”

Every stock has an upper and lower circuit limit (typically 5%, 10%, or 20%) beyond which trading halts for the day. Index-level circuits pause the whole market to prevent panic during crashes. These are retail protections, not bugs.

key_terms.definition: Securities and Exchange Board of India — the market regulator, formed 1992.
Dematerialised account that holds your shares electronically. Required for any stock trading.
Trades settle one working day after execution. India moved from T+2 to T+1 in 2023.
The list of unmatched buy and sell orders at every price level.
Maximum daily % move allowed before trading in a stock is halted.
SEBI-registered intermediary that routes your orders to the exchange.

fields.did_you_know: BSE is Asia's oldest stock exchange, founded in 1875 by Premchand Roychand under a banyan tree in front of Bombay's Town Hall.

fields.title: Stocks, IPOs & Indices Explained
fields.summary: What you actually own when you buy a share, and how indices are built.
fields.body_html:
What a share actually is

When you buy one share of Reliance, you own a literal fractional piece of the company. Reliance has ~676 crore shares outstanding, so each one is 1/676-crore of the whole business — its factories, subsidiaries, contracts, and future profits. Shareholders are the residual owners: after all debts and obligations are paid, whatever's left belongs to them, proportional to ownership.

This ownership gives you two benefits: capital appreciation (share price rises as the business grows) and dividends (a slice of post-tax profits the company chooses to distribute).

How companies become public: the IPO

Before an IPO (Initial Public Offering), a company is private — owned by founders, employees, and early investors. An IPO is the first time its shares are sold to the general public and listed on an exchange.

  • Primary market: the IPO itself — money flows from new investors to the company.
  • Secondary market: every trade after listing — money flows between investors. The company doesn't receive anything.

When you buy shares on Zerodha, you're almost always in the secondary market — trading with another investor, not the company itself.

IPO process in India (simplified)

  1. Company files a DRHP (Draft Red Herring Prospectus) with SEBI.
  2. SEBI reviews and approves.
  3. Price band is set (e.g., ₹90–95).
  4. Public subscription window opens (usually 3–5 days).
  5. Shares are allotted (often by lottery if oversubscribed).
  6. Stock lists on the exchange, often at a premium or discount to IPO price.

What an index is

An index is a basket of stocks that represents a market or segment. Watching the Nifty 50 tells you how the “top 50” are moving without checking each one.

Weighting matters

Most Indian indices use free-float market-cap weighting: bigger companies with more shares freely available get bigger index weight. That's why Reliance Industries alone makes up roughly 10% of the Nifty 50 — a single-day 5% move in Reliance can noticeably move the index.

Major Indian indices

  • Nifty 50 — 50 large-cap stocks across 13 sectors
  • Sensex — BSE's 30-stock flagship
  • Nifty Next 50 — the next 50 after the Nifty 50
  • Nifty Midcap 150 — mid-cap representation
  • Bank Nifty — 12 most liquid banking stocks
  • Nifty IT, FMCG, Pharma, Auto — sector indices

key_terms.definition: Initial Public Offering — a company's first sale of shares to the public.
Shares actually available for public trading (excluding promoter/locked holdings).
Where new shares are issued to investors (IPOs, FPOs, rights issues).
Where existing shares trade between investors — the stock exchange.
Draft Red Herring Prospectus — the detailed SEBI filing before an IPO.
Share price × total shares outstanding. Measures company size.

fields.did_you_know: Reliance Industries alone makes up roughly 10% of the Nifty 50 by weight. A single 5% move in RIL is worth ~50 Nifty points.

fields.title: Fundamental Analysis: PE, EPS, ROE, D/E
fields.summary: Read a company's numbers before you buy. The metrics that actually matter.
fields.body_html:
The mindset

Fundamental analysis tries to answer one question: “Is this a good business at a fair price?” You look at real numbers — revenue, profit, debt, cash flow — not just price charts.

Earnings Per Share (EPS)

EPS = net profit ÷ shares outstanding. It's the profit attributable to each share. Rising EPS year after year is the single most important signal that a business is getting genuinely bigger. Be suspicious of EPS that grows only because the company is buying back shares without growing profit.

Price-to-Earnings (PE) ratio

PE = current price ÷ EPS. Think of it as “years of current earnings you're paying upfront.” A PE of 25 means if earnings stayed flat, you'd recoup your investment in 25 years.

  • PE < 15: cheap — or a value trap (company stagnating)
  • PE 15–25: typical for large Indian companies
  • PE 25–40: growth premium — justified only if earnings are actually growing fast
  • PE > 60: speculative, or near-zero earnings inflating the denominator

PE must be compared within the same sector. IT companies and banks naturally have different PE ranges.

Return on Equity (ROE)

ROE = net profit ÷ shareholder equity. It measures how efficiently the company turns shareholder money into profit.

  • ROE > 15% consistently → high-quality compounder
  • ROE < 10% → capital being poorly used
  • Falling ROE over years → competitive moat eroding

Warren Buffett famously screens for companies with 10+ years of ROE above 15%.

Debt-to-Equity (D/E)

D/E = total debt ÷ equity. Measures leverage.

  • D/E < 0.5: conservative
  • D/E 0.5–1: typical for most industries
  • D/E 1–2: leveraged — rising rates become a real risk
  • D/E > 2: dangerously leveraged, except for banks/NBFCs where it's structurally high

Three more that matter

  • Free Cash Flow (FCF): cash a business generates after reinvesting. A consistently FCF-positive company with rising FCF is a rare gem.
  • Promoter holding: in India, look for promoter stake above 40%. Less than 25% is a warning — insiders don't believe in their own company.
  • Pledging: promoters pledging more than 20% of their shares is a red flag.

Putting it together

A reasonable “good business” screen for Indian large-caps: ROE > 15%, D/E < 1, EPS growing > 10% annually for 5 years, promoter holding > 40%, no pledging. Then worry about PE.

key_terms.definition: Price ÷ EPS. Lower can mean cheaper, but context and sector matter.
Net profit ÷ shareholder equity. >15% consistently is generally healthy.
Total debt ÷ equity. <1 is conservative for most sectors.
Earnings Per Share = net profit ÷ shares outstanding.
Operating cash minus capex — money the business actually produces.
Shares promoters have pledged as loan collateral. >20% is a warning.
Net assets per share. Price-to-book <1 is classically cheap.

fields.did_you_know: Warren Buffett has said he prefers companies with 10+ years of consistent ROE above 15% — that's his primary quality screen before he looks at price.

fields.title: Technical Analysis: Candles, MAs, RSI, MACD
fields.summary: Charts and indicators traders use to time entries and exits.
fields.body_html:
The premise

Technical analysis assumes price already reflects all known information, and the study of price + volume patterns can reveal the probable next move. It's probabilistic, not deterministic — indicators suggest odds, not certainties.

Anatomy of a candlestick

Each candle shows four numbers over a period (1 minute, 1 day, 1 week):

  • Open: first traded price of the period
  • High: highest price reached
  • Low: lowest price reached
  • Close: last traded price

A green candle means close > open (buyers won). A red candle means close < open (sellers won). The thin line above and below (the “wick”) shows how far price travelled before reversing.

Famous patterns

  • Doji: open ≈ close — indecision, often at turning points
  • Hammer: long lower wick, small body near top — buyers fought back
  • Engulfing: a candle fully “eats” the previous one — trend reversal
  • Shooting star: long upper wick at the top — rejection of higher prices

Moving averages

A moving average smooths price. The two most-watched in India:

  • 50-day MA: medium-term trend
  • 200-day MA: long-term trend

When the 50-day crosses above the 200-day, it's a golden cross — classically bullish. The reverse is a death cross.

EMA (exponential MA) weights recent prices more heavily — responds faster but whipsaws more.

RSI (Relative Strength Index)

A momentum oscillator from 0 to 100:

  • > 70: overbought — prices have moved up fast; pullback possible
  • < 30: oversold — prices have fallen fast; bounce possible
  • RSI divergence: price makes new high but RSI doesn't → momentum weakening

Important: in a strong trend, RSI can stay > 70 (or < 30) for weeks. It's not an automatic sell/buy signal — it's a warning flag.

MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence)

Built from EMA crossovers. The classic signals:

  • MACD line crosses above signal line: bullish momentum shift
  • MACD line crosses below signal line: bearish momentum shift
  • Histogram expanding: trend strengthening
  • Histogram contracting: trend losing steam

Bollinger Bands

A 20-day moving average plus two standard deviations on each side. Price touching the upper band doesn't mean “sell” — it means price is unusually high by its own recent standards. Bands that narrow (“squeeze”) often precede a big move in either direction.

Volume — the forgotten indicator

A breakout on low volume usually fails. A breakout on heavy volume is conviction. Always check volume alongside price.

Core rule

Never trade a single indicator. Combine at least 2–3 (e.g., trend via MA, momentum via RSI, confirmation via volume) and wait for alignment. Every indicator lies eventually.

key_terms.definition: Relative Strength Index — momentum oscillator from 0 to 100.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence — trend & momentum indicator.
When the 50-day MA crosses above the 200-day MA (bullish).
50-day MA crosses below the 200-day MA (bearish).
20-day MA + 2 standard deviations — volatility envelope.
Candle with open ≈ close — signals indecision.
Price making new highs/lows while indicator doesn't — momentum warning.

fields.did_you_know: Candlestick charts were invented by Japanese rice trader Munehisa Homma in the 1700s. He reputedly won 100 trades in a row using them.

fields.title: Reading a Balance Sheet
fields.summary: Assets, liabilities, equity — and what they actually tell you.
fields.body_html:
The fundamental equation

Every balance sheet obeys: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. If a company has ₹1,000 crore in assets and ₹600 crore in debts, equity is ₹400 crore — that's what belongs to shareholders on paper.

Assets — what the company owns

  • Current assets (convertible to cash in 12 months): cash, receivables, inventory, short-term investments
  • Non-current assets: property, plant & equipment (PP&E), long-term investments, intangibles, goodwill

Liabilities — what the company owes

  • Current liabilities (due in 12 months): trade payables, short-term borrowings, accrued expenses
  • Non-current liabilities: long-term debt, deferred tax, lease obligations

Equity — what shareholders actually have

  • Share capital (money raised from issuing shares)
  • Reserves (accumulated retained profits)
  • Other components like revaluation or hedge reserves

Key ratios from the balance sheet

  • Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities. Above 1.5 = healthy short-term liquidity.
  • Quick ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities. More conservative.
  • Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ equity.
  • Debt-to-assets = total debt ÷ total assets. How much of the company is funded by debt.

Red flags — things to actively look for

  • Rising receivables outpacing revenue: customers aren't paying on time. Could be a prelude to write-offs.
  • Inventory growing faster than sales: product isn't selling.
  • Sudden goodwill write-downs: management overpaid for an acquisition.
  • Repeated “exceptional items”: management hiding ongoing problems as one-offs.
  • Cash balance that never grows despite “profits”: the profits might only exist on paper. Follow the cash.

Cash flow reconciles the story

A balance sheet tells you position; the cash flow statement tells you how much real money moved. If a company reports high profit but persistently negative operating cash flow, the profits are suspicious. Always cross-check.

The Satyam lesson

Satyam's 2009 fraud — India's Enron — was eventually caught partly because the reported cash on the balance sheet didn't exist in any bank account. Always ask: where is this cash sitting, and would a bank statement confirm it?

key_terms.definition: Short-term liquidity test: current assets ÷ current liabilities.
Like current ratio but excludes inventory (stricter).
Intangible asset from acquisitions — watch for sudden write-downs.
Property, Plant & Equipment — tangible long-term assets.
Money owed to the company by its customers.
Current assets minus current liabilities — short-term operational fuel.

fields.did_you_know: Satyam's 2009 fraud was caught partly because reported cash on the balance sheet (~₹5,000 crore) didn't exist in any bank account — a detail auditors had been signing off on for years.

fields.title: Risk Management & Position Sizing
fields.summary: The boring rules that keep you in the game long enough to get lucky.
fields.body_html:
The math nobody wants to hear

A 10% loss needs an 11% gain to break even. A 30% loss needs a 43% gain. A 50% loss needs a 100% gain. An 80% loss needs a 400% gain. Losses compound non-linearly — that's why protecting downside matters far more than chasing upside.

Rule 1: risk 1–2% per trade, maximum

If your account is ₹5,00,000, don't risk more than ₹5,000–₹10,000 on any single position. This isn't how much you invest — it's how much you're willing to lose if the stop hits.

Position size formula

Position size = (Account size × Risk %) ÷ (Entry price − Stop loss)

Example: Account ₹5,00,000. Risk 1% = ₹5,000. You want to buy TCS at ₹3,800 with a stop at ₹3,700 (₹100 risk per share). Position size = ₹5,000 ÷ ₹100 = 50 shares.

Note how the size depends on the stop distance, not your mood. Tight stops → larger positions. Wide stops → smaller positions. Same risk either way.

Stop losses: before, not after

Always place a stop loss before entering. The moment a trade goes against you is the worst time to think clearly — you'll find reasons to hope. The stop you set in calm saves the account you built.

  • Hard stop: GTT (Good Till Triggered) order on the exchange, cannot be ignored
  • Mental stop: relies on you pressing the button. Most people fail.

ATR-based stops (the pros' choice)

Instead of a fixed 5%, set stops at 2–3 × ATR (Average True Range — 14-day volatility measure). A ₹1,000 stock with ATR ₹20 gets a ₹40–₹60 stop. A ₹1,000 stock with ATR ₹5 gets a ₹10–₹15 stop. You respect the stock's personality instead of one-size-fits-all.

Rule 2: diversify, but don't dilute

  • 1–5 stocks: too concentrated — one wipeout hurts
  • 8–15 stocks across different sectors: the sweet spot for retail Indian portfolios
  • 30+ stocks: you're essentially recreating a mutual fund, with worse fees and more work

Cap any one sector at ~30%. No tech boom ever felt like it could end — until it did.

Rule 3: risk-reward minimums

If your potential profit isn't at least 2× your potential loss, don't take the trade. With a 50% win rate, 1:2 R:R is profitable. With 1:1, you need 55%+ accuracy — hard to achieve.

Rule 4: don't average down losers

“Averaging down” (buying more as price drops) sounds disciplined. It's usually how small losses become big ones. Averaging up into strength is the disciplined version.

Rule 5: journal every trade

Log entry, stop, target, reason, outcome. Review monthly. Patterns emerge: you'll find you lose mostly on Mondays, or on stocks from one sector, or when you skipped the checklist. You cannot improve what you don't measure.

key_terms.definition: Pre-set price at which you exit a losing trade automatically.
Calculating how many shares to buy based on risk tolerance.
Average True Range — 14-day volatility in rupees. Used for dynamic stops.
Potential profit ÷ potential loss. Aim for 2:1 or better.
Good Till Triggered — a standing order on the exchange.
Peak-to-trough drop in account value, usually expressed as %.

fields.did_you_know: A 50% loss requires a 100% gain to break even. An 80% loss requires 400%. Risk math is brutally asymmetric — which is why defence matters more than offence.

fields.title: Mutual Funds & Index Funds
fields.summary: Hands-off investing for beginners (and most pros). Compounding without the drama.
fields.body_html:
The pitch

A mutual fund pools money from thousands of investors and a fund manager uses it to buy a basket of stocks/bonds. You own units of the fund, priced at a daily NAV (Net Asset Value) = (fund's total holdings − fees) ÷ units outstanding.

Types of mutual funds

  • Equity funds: invest mostly in stocks. Higher risk, higher long-term return.
  • Debt funds: invest in bonds/government securities. Lower risk, bond-like returns.
  • Hybrid funds: mix of equity and debt. Balanced risk.
  • Index funds: passively track an index (Nifty 50, Sensex). Low cost.
  • ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds): like index funds but trade on exchanges in real-time.

Active vs passive — the core debate

An active fund has a manager picking stocks trying to beat the index. Fees are typically 1.5–2.5% per year. In the US and increasingly in India, 80%+ of active funds underperform their benchmark over 10 years after fees. In India, the gap is narrowing but many large-cap funds now also underperform.

A passive index fund just buys the index. Zero stock-picking skill needed. Fees: often < 0.2% per year. That 1.5% saving, compounded over 20 years, is enormous.

The expense ratio trap

A fund charging 2% annually takes 2% of your assets every year, whether it performs or not. On ₹10 lakh invested, that's ₹20,000 per year. Over 30 years of compounding at 12%, the difference between a 0.2% and 2% fund is roughly 40% of your final corpus. Fees are the single largest controllable factor in your returns.

Understanding SIP

SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) is simply auto-debiting ₹X every month into a fund. It works because:

  • You buy more units when markets are down, fewer when up — rupee cost averaging.
  • Removes timing anxiety — you invest whether the market is euphoric or terrified.
  • Builds the habit of saving mechanically.

A ₹5,000/month SIP into a Nifty 50 index fund for 30 years, at historical ~12% average, grows to roughly ₹1.75 crore.

ELSS — tax-saving equity funds

ELSS funds qualify for tax deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh under Section 80C. Lock-in: 3 years. Often one of the best tax-saving options for long-term investors.

How to actually choose a fund

  1. Equity corpus of your portfolio: mostly Nifty 50 or Nifty Next 50 index funds. Cheap, boring, effective.
  2. Satellite (optional): mid-cap or flexi-cap fund for slightly higher risk/return.
  3. Debt portion: short-duration debt fund or PPF (safer, guaranteed).
  4. Avoid funds with expense ratio > 1% unless you have a specific thesis.

What SIPs don't do

SIPs don't make bad funds good, they don't guarantee profits, and they don't work if you stop them during market crashes (precisely when you should be buying more). Discipline is the whole game.

key_terms.definition: Systematic Investment Plan — fixed amount auto-invested monthly.
Annual fee charged by the fund as % of assets. Lower is almost always better.
Net Asset Value — per-unit price of a mutual fund.
Equity Linked Savings Scheme — tax-saving equity mutual fund.
Exchange Traded Fund — trades on the exchange like a stock, usually index-tracking.
Buying more when prices are low, less when high, by investing a fixed rupee amount.

fields.did_you_know: John Bogle, who created the first index fund in 1975, was initially mocked — critics called it 'un-American'. It's now a multi-trillion-dollar idea and Vanguard is the largest asset manager in the world.

fields.title: Swing Trading Basics
fields.summary: Holding positions days to weeks — the middle ground between day-trading and investing.
fields.body_html:
What swing trading is

Swing trading aims to capture a “swing” in price — a move that unfolds over 3 days to 3 weeks. It sits between day trading (minutes–hours) and investing (months–years). You're not predicting the next decade; you're playing for the next leg.

The edge you need

You don't need to be right more often — you need your winners to be bigger than your losers. Most successful swing traders win only 40–50% of the time but make 2–3× on winners versus losers. The math still works.

Four setups that have worked for decades

1. Pullback to rising 20-day EMA

In an uptrend, price often retraces to the 20-day EMA before resuming higher. Entry: bounce candle off the EMA with rising volume. Stop: just below the EMA or recent swing low. Target: previous high, then trail.

2. Breakout from consolidation

A stock trades sideways in a tight range for 2–8 weeks, then breaks above the range on heavy volume. Volume is critical — low-volume breakouts fail 70%+ of the time.

3. MACD bullish crossover near zero line

On the daily chart, MACD crossing up through the zero line after a base-building phase is a classical “new uptrend” signal. Combine with price above 50-day MA.

4. Cup-and-handle

Price forms a rounded bottom (the cup), consolidates briefly (the handle), then breaks out. Can last weeks. The deeper the cup, the bigger the move.

Entry checklist (before every trade)

  • Is the broader market (Nifty) in an uptrend? (swing trading works better with the market)
  • Is the stock in an uptrend on the weekly chart?
  • Is volume confirming the signal?
  • Where's my stop loss, and is the risk-reward at least 1:2?
  • What's my position size?
  • What event (earnings, results, budget) could blindside this trade?

Exit rules — the hard part

  • Stop hit: exit, no negotiation.
  • Target hit: scale out 50%, trail the rest.
  • Trailing stop: move stop to break-even once price moves 1R in your favour, then trail below each higher low.
  • Time stop: if the trade isn't working after your expected window, exit even if stop hasn't hit. Dead money is opportunity cost.

What kills swing traders

  • Trading in a sideways market (no clear trends to swing)
  • Ignoring the broader index direction
  • Entering too late, after the move has already run
  • Turning a losing swing trade into a “long-term investment” to avoid booking loss
  • Taking too many positions — 3–5 active positions is plenty

Realistic expectations

A good retail swing trader using 1–2% risk per trade, with a 45% win rate and 1:2.5 R:R, realistically makes 15–30% per year after costs — not 500%. Anyone promising more is selling a course, not a strategy.

key_terms.definition: Price moving decisively above a prior resistance level on volume.
Potential profit ÷ potential loss. Aim for 2:1 or better.
A stop loss that follows price up, locking in gains.
Classical bullish continuation pattern described by William O'Neil.
One unit of risk — how much you'd lose if your stop hit. Profits are often expressed as multiples of R.

fields.did_you_know: Most professional swing traders win on only 40–50% of trades — they make money because their winners are 2–3× the size of their losers. Accuracy is overrated; asymmetry is everything.

fields.title: Options Trading: Intro & Risk Warning
fields.summary: Powerful, leveraged, and unforgiving. Read carefully before touching.
fields.body_html:
READ FIRST: SEBI's January 2023 study found that 89% of retail F&O traders in India lost money in FY2022 — average net loss was ₹1.1 lakh per trader. This module is defensive: understand options so you can avoid being one of those statistics, not so you can rush in.

What an option actually is

An option is a contract that gives you the right (not obligation) to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified price (strike) before a specified date (expiry). You pay a premium for this right.

  • Call option: right to BUY at the strike. You buy calls when bullish.
  • Put option: right to SELL at the strike. You buy puts when bearish.

Concrete example

Reliance is trading at ₹1,400. You buy a 1,450-strike call expiring this Thursday for a premium of ₹20. Each lot is 250 shares, so you pay 20 × 250 = ₹5,000.

  • If Reliance expires at ₹1,500: your call is worth ₹50 intrinsically. Your profit = (50 − 20) × 250 = ₹7,500 (150% in a week).
  • If Reliance expires at ₹1,440: your call is worth ₹0. You lose the full ₹5,000 premium.
  • If Reliance expires at ₹1,450: intrinsically worth 0. You lose ₹5,000.

Notice: even a small move in the wrong direction — or no move at all — causes total loss of premium. Time is the enemy.

The four Greeks (briefly)

  • Delta: how much the option price changes per ₹1 change in underlying.
  • Theta: how much the option loses per day from time decay. Always negative for buyers.
  • Vega: sensitivity to volatility changes.
  • Gamma: rate of change of delta.

You don't need these to survive — but you should understand that theta means you lose money every day even if nothing happens. This is the #1 reason retail option buyers lose.

Buying vs selling options

  • Buying (long): max loss = premium. Max gain = theoretically unlimited for calls, very large for puts. Time works against you.
  • Selling (short / writing): max gain = premium. Max loss = theoretically unlimited for naked calls, very large for naked puts. Time works for you. Requires large margin.

Never sell naked options as a beginner. One gap-down on an index can blow up the entire account.

Common traps

  • Far OTM (Out-of-the-money) options on expiry day — they look cheap; they expire worthless 90% of the time.
  • Holding through events: IV (implied volatility) collapses post-event, crushing premium even if you were right on direction.
  • Revenge trading after a loss. Losses compound fastest in options.

If you must, start here

  1. Paper trade for 3 months. Track every trade.
  2. Only buy options, never sell, until you've read 2+ books (Natenberg; McMillan).
  3. Position-size so one loss = max 2% of account.
  4. Only trade liquid indices (Nifty, Bank Nifty) initially — single-stock options can have spreads that eat profit.
  5. Avoid expiry day as a beginner — too much gamma risk.

The honest answer

For 99% of retail investors, options offer worse risk-adjusted returns than plain equity or mutual funds. The leverage is seductive; the losses are asymmetric. If you want excitement, gamble 1% of your net worth. Compound the other 99% in an index fund.

key_terms.definition: The price at which the option can be exercised.
What you pay to buy the option contract.
Selling an option without owning the underlying — extremely risky.
Time decay — how much an option loses per day from time passing.
Change in option price per ₹1 move in the underlying.
Implied Volatility — the market's expectation of future volatility, priced into the option.
The date the option ceases to exist. Weekly for Nifty/Bank Nifty.
Number of shares per contract. Nifty: 50; Bank Nifty: 35; Reliance: 250 (varies).

fields.did_you_know: SEBI's 2023 study found that 89% of retail F&O traders in India lost money — average net loss was ₹1.1 lakh per trader. The exchanges made ₹1,250 crore in transaction fees from those same loss-making trades.

fields.title: How to Start Investing at 18 in India
fields.summary: PAN, demat, broker — the practical setup and your first 12 months.
fields.body_html:
Step 1 — Get your PAN card

The PAN (Permanent Account Number) is a 10-character alphanumeric ID issued by the Income Tax department. You cannot open any investment account in India without it. Apply online at the NSDL or UTIITSL portals — takes 10–15 days, costs ~₹100. Keep the physical card safe.

Step 2 — Open a demat + trading account

A demat account holds your shares electronically; a trading account lets you buy and sell. Most brokers bundle both. India's popular online-only brokers in 2026:

  • Zerodha — the original discount broker, clean UI, excellent education
  • Groww — friendliest for beginners, mutual funds + stocks
  • Upstox — competitive pricing, decent app
  • Dhan — powerful tools for active traders
  • Angel One — full-service with research

You'll need: PAN, Aadhaar, bank account, signature, a selfie, and a cancelled cheque / bank statement. Fully online via DigiLocker e-KYC. Typically approved in 24–48 hours.

Step 3 — Link your bank account

All money flows: Your Bank → Broker → Exchange → Broker → Your Bank. Link the bank account via UPI or netbanking from inside the broker's app. Most brokers support instant UPI deposits.

Step 4 — Your first investment

Don't pick a stock yet. Start with this:

  1. Set up a SIP of ₹500–2,000/month into a Nifty 50 index fund. Any of: UTI Nifty 50, Nippon India Nifty 50, HDFC Nifty 50. Expense ratios under 0.20%.
  2. This does three things: forces the habit, learns you the mechanics, and builds real wealth quietly.
  3. Ignore it for 3 months. Seriously.

Step 5 — Read while your SIP compounds

Before touching individual stocks, read:

  • The Psychology of Money — Morgan Housel (short, readable, changes how you think)
  • One Up on Wall Street — Peter Lynch (classic, still relevant)
  • Coffee Can Investing — Saurabh Mukherjea (Indian context)
  • Bulls, Bears and Other Beasts — Santosh Nair (history of Indian markets)

Step 6 — Your first stock (after 6–12 months)

Pick one company you actually understand — whose product you use daily — and buy ₹5,000 worth. Tata Consumer, HUL, ITC, HDFC Bank, Asian Paints — anything boring is fine. Hold it for a year. Watch how it behaves through earnings, news, and panics. This is tuition.

Step 7 — The tax bit

  • STCG (Short-term capital gains, < 12 months): taxed at 20% (rates updated post-2024 budget).
  • LTCG (Long-term capital gains, > 12 months): ₹1.25 lakh exempt per year; 12.5% above that.
  • Dividends are taxed at your slab rate.
  • Use an ITR-2 or ITR-3 to file if you have capital gains. CA help is worth it in year 1.

Step 8 — Set up the right protections

  • Emergency fund first: 6 months of expenses in a liquid fund or savings account. Investing without this is building on sand.
  • Term insurance: only if you have dependents.
  • Health insurance: even if your parents have one, get your own by 25.

What not to do in year 1

  • No F&O (SEBI says 89% lose money).
  • No crypto with borrowed money.
  • No “hot tip” small-caps from Telegram groups.
  • No leverage of any kind.
  • Don't watch CNBC all day. Watch your SIP compound instead.

Where you should be in 3 years

If you start at 18 with a ₹2,000/month SIP and raise it 10% each year, you'll have roughly ₹90,000 invested by age 21, worth ₹1.1–1.3 lakh at historical returns. Boring? Yes. But you'll have built the most valuable thing — the habit. Compounding only works if you let it.
